video_title: The Bull Market Is Back! But Bitcoin Isn’t Leading It?
gist: Bankless hosts Ryan and David argue a new crypto bull market has been confirmed by on-chain and technical signals (golden cross, holder-cohort reset, reclaimed 50-week MA), but this cycle's leadership looks different: revenue-generating tokens (Athena, Uniswap, Ondo, Jupiter, Arbitrum) and store-of-value challenger Zcash are outperforming Bitcoin, which currently lacks a clear marginal buyer. They also cover a Kalshi wash-trading scandal, a Howard Marks memo urging crypto as a dollar-debasement hedge, and a wave of new institutional products (Variational TGE, Ondo/BlackRock vaults, Binance's stake in Circle).

insights.claim: The golden cross (50-day moving average crossing above the 200-day moving average) confirmed on Bitcoin this week, a signal that in previous cycles has marked the transition out of the bear market into the early bull phase.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Michael Nato)
insights.so_what: Golden cross confirmation is one of several technical triggers analysts use to time bull-market entry; watch for it to hold alongside other confirming signals rather than trading on it alone.

insights.claim: Bitcoin reclaimed its 50-week moving average (currently at $78,800) two to three months after the cycle low, matching the historical pattern seen at the start of prior bull phases; a monthly close above that level is viewed as a bottom-confirmation signal.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Michael Nato)
insights.so_what: Investors can track monthly closes above $78.8k as a rule-based confirmation that the bear market has ended; repeated failure to hold it would undercut the early-bull thesis.

insights.claim: This bear cycle was unusually shallow versus the last one: Bitcoin only traded 5-8% below its 200-week moving average this time, compared to being roughly 35% below it for an extended period in the prior bear market, attributed to less systemic leverage/debt in the system this cycle (no Terra/Luna, no Three Arrows Capital, no FTX-style contagion).
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: A sustained multi-month close below the current 200-week moving average (~$65,500) would be the clearest signal that the early-bull thesis has broken, since it would replicate the depth of the prior, more contagion-driven bear market.
insights.quote: The furthest we ever got below was about 5 to 8%.

insights.claim: Crypto analyst Ben Cowan publicly admitted his bearish Q4 2026 thesis was wrong: he expected rising energy prices to push long-end rates up, the Fed to hike in September, the dollar to strengthen, and Bitcoin to reprice downward as a result — none of which materialized, and Bitcoin rallied through the rate move instead.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host, citing Ben Cowan)
insights.so_what: Even sophisticated four-year-cycle analysts were wrong-footed by over-indexing on macro variables; treat macro-driven Bitcoin price calls with skepticism relative to on-chain/holder-behavior signals.
insights.quote: my thesis was that rising energy prices would cause the long end to go up then they would raise rates in September then the dollar would go up and Bitcoin would repric because of the rate hike

insights.claim: A CoinDesk analysis found the correlation between 10-year Treasury yields and Bitcoin is only about -0.18, indicating rising bond yields have essentially no reliable predictive relationship with Bitcoin's price over the long term.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host, citing CoinDesk)
insights.so_what: Investors using rising 10-year/30-year yields as a bearish Bitcoin signal are relying on a weak historical correlation; the current all-time-high bond yields are not, by themselves, a strong reason to expect Bitcoin downside.
insights.quote: the correlation between the 10-year yields and Bitcoin is at 0.18 inverse

insights.claim: An alternate bullish read circulating on crypto Twitter (attributed to Felix of Forward Guidance) holds that record Treasury yields (5.15% 10-year, 5.44% 30-year) reflect a strong economy pulling capital toward growth assets/equities rather than a fiscal-crisis warning — i.e., yields are rising because everyone wants to deploy capital into growth, not because bonds are being shunned out of fear.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Felix/Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: If this bullish read is correct, high yields could coexist with rising risk-asset prices rather than choke them off; worth tracking whether equity/crypto strength persists alongside continued yield increases as a test of this thesis.
insights.quote: what if the bond market is you know printing in five six 7% because the economy is cooking

themes.theme: Whose bull market: revenue rotation vs. Bitcoin

insights.claim: This week's biggest crypto gainers — Athena (+40%), Uniswap (+30%), Ondo (+30%), Jupiter (+30%), and Arbitrum (+30%) — all share one trait: they generate real protocol revenue/fee income, unlike ETH which was only up 9% despite being considered a blue-chip.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Revenue/fee-generation is emerging as the dominant factor driving outperformance this cycle; screening for tokens with real cash-flow-like mechanics (fee burns, buybacks) may be a more useful filter than market-cap tier or narrative alone.
insights.quote: They make money. They all print revenue.

insights.claim: Arbitrum was the only Layer-2 token to rally this week, and it did so specifically because it captures 10% of Robinhood Chain's fees — not because of any broader Layer-2 narrative, distinguishing this pump from prior cycles' generic L2 rallies.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: The Arbitrum rally is a company-specific revenue story (Robinhood Chain fee capture), not a sector-wide L2 re-rating, so other L2 tokens shouldn't be assumed to follow without their own revenue catalyst.
insights.quote: it's pumping because of its ties to revenue from the Robin Hood chain that you can clearly see

insights.claim: Delphi Digital data (referenced from a June tweet) showed a basket of revenue-generating crypto assets up roughly 17% over a period in which blue chips Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana were down about 30%, and the hosts say this divergence has only widened since.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Delphi Digital)
insights.so_what: Revenue-generating altcoins have structurally decoupled from blue-chip performance since at least June 2026; this basket-vs-blue-chip divergence is a trackable trade for relative-value positioning.

insights.claim: Bankless publisher David Feld argued in a newsletter piece titled 'This is not Bitcoin's cycle' that Bitcoin lacks cash flow (unlike the newly outperforming revenue tokens) and lacks an obvious next marginal buyer this cycle, since Michael Saylor's Strategy already holds all the BTC it wants and there is no repeat of the 2024 ETF-driven institutional buying wave.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host, citing David Feld)
insights.so_what: If Bitcoin genuinely lacks a marginal buyer this cycle, its historical pattern of leading early-cycle dominance gains before alts follow may not repeat, favoring relative allocation toward revenue-generating alts over BTC.

insights.claim: Bitcoin dominance is currently around 59% of total crypto market cap; the historical pattern is for Bitcoin dominance to rise early in a bull cycle before alts catch up later, and the hosts are questioning whether that sequence will hold this cycle given the current alt/revenue-token strength.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: A break from the usual BTC-dominance-rises-first pattern this early in the cycle would itself be a signal that this cycle's capital-flow dynamics are structurally different from 2020-2021 and 2023-2024.

insights.claim: Despite the revenue-token rotation, the hosts note a separate durable bid for Bitcoin may persist from non-crypto-native, debasement-focused institutional allocators (citing macro commentator Michael Howell's framing of Bitcoin as roughly a '5x levered gold' position) who buy on a 10-plus year horizon rather than based on cash flow.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Michael Howell)
insights.so_what: Long-horizon debasement-hedge buyers represent a structurally different, less cycle-sensitive demand source for Bitcoin than crypto-native rotation flows, and could keep providing a bid even if BTC underperforms cash-flow tokens in the near term.

insights.claim: Zcash's market capitalization exceeded $26 billion as of the week of this recording, up from roughly $200 million-$300 million about a year earlier (per the hosts), making it one of the fastest market-cap expansions in the sector this cycle despite having no cash-flow/revenue mechanism.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Zcash's growth trajectory (sub-$1B to $26B in under a year) makes it a legitimate emerging store-of-value asset to track alongside Bitcoin and Ethereum, independent of any revenue-based investment thesis.

insights.claim: The Zcash rally is being driven by existing Bitcoin holders rotating a small slice (roughly 1%) of their BTC market cap into ZEC rather than by Ethereum or Solana capital, with names like the Winklevoss twins, Barry Silbert, and Grayscale cited as involved in that rotation.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Because Zcash's bid is coming from Bitcoin's own holder base rather than new external capital, its growth ceiling is partly a function of how much more of Bitcoin's ~$1.7 trillion market cap continues to rotate into it.
insights.quote: It's Bitcoiners shaving off like 1% of their market cap.

insights.claim: The hosts identify Zcash and NEAR as a pairing worth watching together: Zcash is competing for Bitcoin's 'private money/store of value' trophy while NEAR is competing for the 'smart contract platform' trophy previously held by Ethereum and then Solana, both via a privacy-focused thesis (Zcash's private transactions, NEAR's confidential cross-chain intents).
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: NEAR was up 54% in seven days and intents volume was up 85% in two weeks, per the hosts, making it a candidate second-tier bet on the same 'privacy meta' rotation that has driven Zcash.
insights.quote: near is the biggest mover of the week this week is up 54% uh in 7 days

insights.claim: NEAR is running an 'ultrasound money' style buy-and-burn mechanism where roughly 60% of NEAR token issuance is being offset by burns funded from confidential-intents revenue, a mechanic the hosts say echoes Ethereum's abandoned 'ultrasound money' narrative from its post-Merge low-price period.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: A revenue-funded burn rate near 60% of issuance is a concrete, trackable supply-side metric for NEAR that ties directly into the broader 'revenue tokens are outperforming' thesis for this cycle.

insights.claim: A Twitter user (Benny) presented evidence that Kalshi's ETH perpetual market saw about $500 million in daily traded volume against only $3.1 million in open interest — a roughly 174x daily turnover ratio that the hosts describe as an implausible dislocation consistent with wash trading.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: A 174x volume-to-open-interest ratio is a concrete red flag investors/traders can use to judge whether reported volume on a derivatives venue reflects genuine price discovery or manufactured activity.
insights.quote: there's half a billion dollar traded hands on the volume on the ETH perpetual. The open interest is 3.1 million.

insights.claim: The Wall Street Journal reported nearly 1 million near-identical $5,500 trades on Kalshi accounting for more than $5 billion of volume in a single month, corroborating the wash-trading allegations first raised on Twitter.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Wall Street Journal)
insights.so_what: Independent confirmation by a mainstream outlet (WSJ) elevates this from a Twitter dispute to a credibility risk for Kalshi's reported volume and market-share claims versus competitors like Polymarket.

insights.claim: Bloomberg previously reported that Jump Trading was given an equity ownership stake in Kalshi while also being permitted to market-make on the platform and receive volume-based fee rebates, creating a direct financial incentive for a designated market maker to inflate trading volume.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Bloomberg)
insights.so_what: A market maker holding equity in the venue it trades on, combined with fee rebates, is a structural conflict of interest that should factor into how much weight investors give Kalshi's self-reported volume and market-share figures.

insights.claim: On the prediction-market side of its business, Kalshi has been reporting contract volume with an added dollar sign (e.g., 100,000 contracts trading at 30 cents each reported as if $100,000 changed hands, when only $30,000 actually did), inflating its stated dollar volume by more than 3x versus the real notional traded.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Kalshi's headline prediction-market volume and market-share numbers (e.g., its claimed 96.7% share of regulated on-shore volume versus Polymarket) should be treated skeptically given this reporting methodology.

insights.claim: Kalshi's public response to the wash-trading allegations characterized the repeated $5,500 trades as one paid market maker quoting fixed sizes to hundreds of distinct takers, but the hosts note the response does not address several of the other specific pieces of evidence raised, leaving the story unresolved as of this recording (with the CFTC stated as not investigating).
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Kalshi's only partial rebuttal, combined with an ongoing lack of CFTC action, means the reputational and regulatory overhang on Kalshi is a live risk factor for anyone evaluating or trading through the platform.
insights.quote: the repeated $5,500 tickets are one paid market maker quoting fixed sizes hundreds of distinct takers

themes.theme: Howard Marks memo: yields and dollar debasement

insights.claim: In a memo titled 'Shall We Repeal the Law of Economics,' bond investor Howard Marks attributes record US Treasury yields (10-year at 5.15%, 30-year at 5.44%, both multi-decade highs) to three causes: persistently high inflation (PCE around 3.7% versus the Fed's 2% target), zero US fiscal discipline (roughly $40 trillion in federal debt with about $1 trillion in annual interest payments now exceeding US military spending), and a capital demand squeeze from roughly $5 trillion in AI datacenter buildout competing with about $2 trillion of Treasury issuance for available capital.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Howard Marks)
insights.so_what: Marks's framework gives investors three concrete, trackable variables (PCE inflation, US debt/interest-to-GDP trends, and AI capex debt issuance) to monitor as drivers of the yield backdrop that in turn affects the relative attractiveness of debasement hedges like crypto and gold.

insights.claim: Howard Marks explicitly named cryptocurrencies as one viable hedge against dollar debasement in his memo, alongside non-dollar currencies, gold, non-US real estate, and non-US equities, while noting the other options each have their own drawbacks (other currencies also debase; non-US companies are relatively scarce and inferior to strong US performers).
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Howard Marks)
insights.so_what: A mainstream, widely-followed bond investor naming crypto as a legitimate debasement hedge in a formal memo is a notable credibility signal that can be cited when making the institutional case for crypto allocation.
insights.quote: he says cryptocurrencies. He actually mentioned cryptocurrencies in the memo.

insights.claim: Howard Marks advised against selling US stocks despite the fiscal/debasement concerns, arguing the problem lies with US government fiscal management and the dollar, not with the quality of American companies, which he characterizes as strong.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host, citing Howard Marks)
insights.so_what: Marks's distinction implies a barbell approach — stay long quality US equities for corporate fundamentals while separately hedging currency/fiscal risk via gold, crypto, or non-US real assets — rather than exiting US equities outright.
insights.quote: The problem we face isn't a problem with the US stock market or with US companies. The problem is with the US fiscal management and ultimately it's a problem with the US dollar.

insights.claim: Variational, a financial-instrument aggregator spanning perpetuals, options, and spot across both on-chain and traditional-finance market-maker liquidity, announced a token generation event airdropping 32% of token supply, with 100% of protocol revenue directed to a treasury that buys back and burns the VAR token (a Hyperliquid/Lighter-style tokenomics model).
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: The 100%-revenue-to-buyback design mirrors the mechanic credited with Hyperliquid's token performance; investors evaluating the Variational airdrop/TGE should weigh the same revenue-capture thesis that has driven other fee-burn tokens this cycle.

insights.claim: Ondo Finance and BlackRock launched 'Intelligent Portfolios,' single tokenized vaults that wrap Ondo's tokenized real-world assets into three model strategies (high income, diversified growth, and high growth) built using BlackRock's proprietary asset-allocation models.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: This is a concrete example of a major institutional asset manager (BlackRock) packaging its allocation methodology directly into an on-chain tokenized product, a template other asset managers may follow for distributing model portfolios on-chain.

insights.claim: BlackRock published a report arguing that as AI represents 'machine-native intelligence,' digital assets/crypto represent the 'machine-native money' AI systems will need, framing crypto's success as tied to AI's success — a narrative being pushed to BlackRock's roughly $10 trillion in institutional assets under management and client base.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host, citing BlackRock)
insights.so_what: A $10 trillion AUM manager actively distributing an AI-needs-crypto narrative to its institutional client base is a notable tailwind for continued institutional crypto adoption and narrative validation this cycle.
insights.quote: digital assets represent machine native money

insights.claim: Binance took a $100 million equity stake in Circle (1.24 million shares at a 5% discount with a two-year lockup) alongside a separate five-year deal in which Circle pays Binance monthly incentives on USDC balances held on the exchange.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: The deal signals Binance moving further into the US-regulated financial system and gives Circle a second major USDC distribution partner beyond Coinbase, potentially reducing Circle's negotiating-leverage dependence on the Coinbase relationship.

insights.claim: Coinbase opened up IPO share allocations to US retail investors, starting with the Aura smart-ring IPO, extending Coinbase's push toward feature parity with Robinhood on the equities/brokerage side of its product.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Coinbase's expansion into retail IPO access and equities is a incremental data point on its diversification beyond crypto trading revenue, competing more directly with Robinhood's product suite.

insights.claim: Vitalik Buterin publicly endorsed the prediction market Truo (which is moving from the Base L2 back to Ethereum's L1), praising it as dedicated to decentralization and ethics without the 'corpo slop' he associates with rivals; the token pumped roughly 10x following the tweet, though it remains a micro-cap around $8-10 million with only about $1-2 million in total value locked.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host, citing Vitalik Buterin)
insights.so_what: A Vitalik endorsement can drive a 10x short-term price move even on a token with minimal TVL/usage, illustrating how much narrative/influencer weight still moves micro-cap crypto prices independent of fundamentals.
insights.quote: Glad to see that Ethereum L1 will have a new strong prediction market contender that is dedicated to decentralization and being ethical and not corpos

insights.claim: Earlier in 2026, Vitalik Buterin criticized the prediction-market sector broadly for over-converging on short-term cryptocurrency price bets and sports-betting-style 'dopamine' products rather than delivering the long-term informational or societal value he originally envisioned for prediction markets going back to Augur circa 2015-2016.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Bankless host, citing Vitalik Buterin)
insights.so_what: Vitalik's critique implicitly targets the dominant, high-volume players (implicitly Polymarket and Kalshi) as having sacrificed the sector's original information-value thesis for engagement-driven betting products, a framing investors can use to separate 'mission-aligned' from 'traction-driven' prediction-market bets.
insights.quote: prediction markets were overconverging to an unhealthy product market fit, embracing short-term cryptocurrency price bets, the sports betting, the dopamine stuff, not the kind of long-term fulfillment or societal information value

insights.claim: The hosts describe a recurring tension in crypto between building for 'virtue' (decentralization/ethics with minimal traction, e.g., Truo's ~$1-2M TVL) versus building for 'traction' (compromising on decentralization to win usage, e.g., Tether's dominance over more decentralized stablecoin alternatives like RAI), arguing that virtue without market validation produces unused protocols.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: This virtue-vs-traction framework is a useful lens for evaluating any new 'ethical alternative' token launch: a values-aligned narrative and an initial price pump do not by themselves indicate durable product-market fit or investment merit.
